title: Arrhenius parameter scatter within uncertainty bounds
summary: For each reaction, a bar for the prior uncertainty range with a marker for the starting value and the optimised value of log A, n and Ea. It tells whether an optimiser stayed inside what the kinetics literature allows.

media.alt: Three panels of horizontal bars for eight reactions showing prior bounds, initial and optimised values of log A, temperature exponent and activation energy.
media.caption: Reference render with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery).

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Are optimized A, n, Ea inside prior ranges?
read_the_figure.axes: Three panels sharing the reaction axis (R1 to R8 on y). x: log10 A in cm, mol, s units; n, the temperature exponent (dimensionless); Ea in kJ/mol.
look_at: Are all teal circles (optimised) inside the grey bars?
Which reactions end with a red cross outside the bars? (R6 for log A, R3 for Ea here.)
How far did the optimiser move from the blue squares (initial)?
Are the bars of unequal width, and does a narrow bar mean a well-known rate?
read_the_figure.proves: An optimised mechanism whose parameters all sit inside the prior bounds is physically plausible. A parameter outside its bounds says the optimiser compensated a structural error somewhere else.
if_wrong: Bounds not drawn: no way to tell a valid fit from an over-fit.
Parameters piled at the edge of a bar: the bound is active, the optimum is probably outside.
Each panel on its own: but A, n and Ea are correlated, and a shift in one is compensated by another.

terms.meaning: The constant A in the Arrhenius law, with units that depend on the reaction order. Plotted as log10 A.
The n in the modified Arrhenius law k = A T^n exp(-Ea / RT).
Energy barrier in the Arrhenius law, here in kJ/mol.
Range of a parameter allowed by independent knowledge (measurements, theory), often as a factor in k.
The parameter after fitting the mechanism to targets such as ignition delays.

remember: k = A T^n exp(-Ea / R T), parameters in this order and units.
Grey bar = allowed range; blue square = start; teal = end; red cross = outside.
A, n and Ea compensate each other: judge the rate k, not one parameter.
One factor of 10 in A is one unit on the log10 A axis.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position along each panel's x encodes the parameter value, position on y encodes the reaction. The grey bar with caps encodes the prior range, a blue square the initial value, a circle the optimised value, and a red X marks an optimised value that falls outside. Shared y across panels lines up each reaction across the three parameters.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: A mechanism fit has dozens of parameters, each with its own allowed interval. A strip per reaction gives each parameter a comparison on its own common scale: inside or outside, near the centre or at the edge. The eye is good at 'is the dot between the caps'. Compact repetition across A, n and Ea makes the pattern across parameters obvious.

understand.title: Read this reference render
understand.text: Q1: How many optimised values are outside? Two: log A for R6 (marker at about 14.3, past a bar that ends near 14.0) and Ea for R3 (about 87 kJ/mol against a bar ending near 81). Q2: How far did R1's log A move? From about 13.3 (blue square) to about 13.8 (teal circle), half a decade, so the rate rose by a factor of 10^0.5, about 3, at fixed n and Ea. Q3: Which reaction is best known? R5 on Ea: its bar spans only about 48 to 74 kJ/mol, the narrowest of the set.

understand.title: The must-check list, explained
understand.text: Bounds drawn: the grey bars are the whole content of the check. A fit plot without them cannot tell inside from outside and must be rejected.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Each panel has its own x scale, so bars of equal length can stand for different relative uncertainties. The marginal view ignores correlation: a point may be inside every bar and still give a rate far outside the allowed rate window. Bounds taken as a box are not the true prior, which is often Gaussian in log k. If bounds are widened after the fact the plot is meaningless.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A plot of the resulting rate k(T) against T with the uncertainty band shows the quantity that matters. A scatter of Ea against log A with a confidence ellipse shows the correlation. A table of fitted values and bounds is exact.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add the factor uncertainty f next to each reaction, and a fourth panel with the rate constant at 1000 K and its allowed band.

steps.title: Modified Arrhenius law
steps.note: The three parameters on the three panels.

steps.title: Effect of an Ea shift at a given temperature
steps.note: Moving Ea by 15 kJ/mol at 1000 K changes k by a factor of about 6 (use the minus sign for an increase).

worked.title: What a boundary excursion means for the rate
worked.problem: R3's optimised Ea is 87 kJ/mol against an upper bound of 81 kJ/mol. At 1000 K by what factor does k change if A and n are fixed?
worked.answer: k is about 0.49 of its value at the bound: the excursion halves the rate at 1000 K, so a compensating change in A would be needed.

checks.q: What do the three kinds of marker mean?
checks.answer: Blue square initial, teal circle optimised inside bounds, red cross optimised outside bounds.

checks.q: log10 A rises from 13.3 to 13.8 at fixed n and Ea. By what factor does k change?
checks.hint: 10 to the power of the difference.

checks.q: R3 and R6 are the only two violations, in different parameters. Does that suggest a problem in the mechanism or in the optimiser set-up?
checks.hint: Which reactions matter most per the sensitivity chart?
checks.answer: Look first at whether R3 and R6 are high-sensitivity reactions; if so the data are pressing the fit against the bound, which hints at a structural error elsewhere in the mechanism.
